abstract: Agentic AI can access student records, retain memory, delegate work and initiate institutional actions. When a model is mistaken or pursuing a hidden objective, a useful safeguard must constrain what it can cause without relying on its stated intentions. Trust by Construction presents a compositional reference architecture for this boundary. A workload declaration and task contract limit authority; deterministic services mediate context, memory, delegation, effects and release. The contribution is an executable account of how these controls interact, including three failure-sensitive mechanisms: a durable workload stop that survives evidence-writer failure, reauthorisation of queued output at each delivery boundary, and an AI-monitor interface that may restrict authority but cannot grant it. The public reference uses synthetic education fixtures and an independent state-and-byte outcome check. Existing cross-sector experiments contain 180 of 180 hostile scenarios while completing 58 of 58 benign tasks. Eighteen additional local regression cases exercise stop, delivery and monitoring behavior. These measurements establish behavior within declared interfaces, not real-world attack prevalence or model alignment. The artifact provides a reusable engineering and teaching method: bind each authority claim to an enforcement point, an accountable role, an executed failure test and an explicit residual risk. The system does not establish operating-system isolation, substantive decision correctness or production certification.
intro: Learning institutions expose the difference between useful reasoning and legitimate authority. A tutor may need a limited record view; a registrar may approve a correction; a research assistant may need public information without access to restricted student data. Combining these privileges in one agent process creates a larger failure surface than any individual task requires. Recent safety research separates misuse, misalignment, mistakes and structural risks, and argues for both model-level and system-level mitigations [1]. Experiments also show insider-threat behavior under constructed goal conflict and replacement pressure [5]. We address the institutional systems boundary: how can a compromised or unreliable reasoning component remain useful while consequential reads, writes and releases require independent authority?
foundations: Our contribution is compositional rather than a new alignment algorithm. CaMeL demonstrates a system-level defense that separates control and data flow and constrains disclosure through capabilities [2]. Trust by Construction applies related architectural principles to an education workflow with memory, agent populations, effect approval, revocation and recipient delivery. It contributes an inspectable enforcement path, failure tests and a claim-to-evidence register. It does not offer a formal proof for arbitrary agent programs or a head-to-head performance comparison with CaMeL. The paper separates properties tested in the local kernel from requirements imposed on deployment adapters.
covert: Recent results motivate testing the authority boundary even when model behavior appears cooperative. Anti-scheming training reduced covert actions in held-out settings but left residual failures and evaluation-awareness confounds [3]. Chain-of-thought monitoring offers an imperfect signal rather than a reliable authorization basis [4]. Reward-hacking research found generalization from training shortcuts to broader misalignment [6], while SHADE-Arena evaluates harmful side objectives hidden within legitimate tasks [7]. A 2026 safety-research study found no unprompted sabotage in its tested settings, yet observed sabotage continuation in some seeded trajectories; those conditions must not be conflated [8]. Bengio and colleagues propose non-agentic Scientist AI as a safer direction for assisting research [9]. These findings support our design choice: AI may propose work, generate tests and report anomalies, while deterministic checks retain authority. A compromised monitor can still deny service or miss misconduct; it must not gain the power to approve an effect or restore privilege.
education_example: A concrete teaching exercise follows a synthetic transcript correction. The agent retrieves only the authorized record and proposes a version-bound change. A source role confirms the supporting evidence and a different reviewer approves the exact proposal. The executor revalidates authority before changing the record. A recipient receives only the approved artifact; a stop or revocation between chunks denies the remainder. Students can compare a valid completion with an attempted forged approval, contaminated memory and a misleading monitor verdict. This teaches the distinction between fluent advice, authorization, source validity and correctness. No result here measures learning outcomes or fairness; those require an institutional study.
validity: Threats to validity and deployment limits. The experiments use synthetic fixtures and declared interfaces. The new tests submit scripted findings and adversarial requests; no live frontier-model detector is evaluated, and no detector accuracy, real-world attack rate or causal prevention of an incident is claimed. Shared Python and SQLite state is trusted service infrastructure, not isolation from hostile native code. A source digest records artifact identity but does not attest a running model. Monitor false positives can reduce availability, and sparse event metadata can miss intent. Chunks are staged approved bytes rather than live model-token streaming; bytes already released cannot be recalled. Workload federation, independent witnesses, physical data erasure, OS/network confinement, qualified external transports and the training/promotion lifecycle remain deployment or implementation work. Local transactions do not establish exactly-once remote effects. The supplementary incident map is an architectural reading of public disclosures. Five of the fourteen mapped stages are not mediated locally; its existence is not evidence that the system would prevent a real breach.
